Right: the same graph with the edge between B and C pointing the other way (shown in the accent color); no path returns to its start any more, so has_cycles() returns False." width="100%"} For directed graphs, uses depth-first search to look for back edges. For undirected graphs, walking an edge and straight back does not count: a cycle needs three or more distinct nodes, a self-loop, or two parallel edges between the same pair of nodes. Trees and paths are therefore acyclic. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if the graph contains at least one cycle, `False` if acyclic. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#0d0e89e5 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) ) graph.has_cycles() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` False ``` ::: ::: Adding an edge back from "C" to "A" closes the loop, so the graph now contains a cycle: ::: {#e0bab4bf .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.add_edge("C", "A") graph.has_cycles() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` True ``` ::: :::
